turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. So, um, the reason I made the appointment... well, it’s honestly getting a bit embarrassing, but I just keep getting up when I am absolutely supposed to stay put. It sounds like something a restless kid would do, right? But I’m 49 years old, and I just can't seem to stay in my chair. 

I’m a private investigator, which means I do a lot of client interviews. People come to me, usually very stressed or upset, and they need to tell me all these highly sensitive details. I’m supposed to be this grounded, attentive professional. But right in the middle of them pouring their hearts out, I’ll just... stand up. I’ll start pacing behind my desk, or I’ll go fiddle with the window blinds, or I’ll offer them water for the third time just to have an excuse to move. 

And it’s not just at work! I do some tutoring on the side, and I’m constantly popping out of my seat and hovering around the room instead of just sitting next to the student. Even at my book club—we meet once a month, usually at my friend Diane's house, and she has these very comfortable couches—but I can't just sit on them. Everyone else is settled in with their wine, discussing the chapters, and there I am, wandering over to the kitchen island or standing behind the sofa. 

People are really starting to notice. My clients, my friends... they give me these looks, and it’s becoming really obvious to everyone that I just can't sit and listen. It makes it seem like I don't care about what they're saying, even though I *am* listening! I just can't seem to do it while sitting down. So, yeah, that's what brings me in today. I need to figure out why I can't just stay in my seat.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they repeatedly get up and leave their chair during situations where they are expected to remain seated, such as client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club meetings.

turns.doctor_question: Have you started or increased any antipsychotic or anti-nausea medicine recently?
turns.patient_response:
Antipsychotic or anti-nausea? Oh, um, no. No, definitely not. I haven't started anything new like that at all. I mean, I really don't take much in the way of medication anyway. Just a standard multivitamin in the mornings, usually with my coffee—which, I know, I read this article recently that said the tannins in coffee can actually block vitamin absorption, so maybe I should stop doing that, but it’s just so ingrained in my morning routine, you know? 

But no, absolutely no antipsychotics. And as for anti-nausea medicine, I actually have an absolute iron stomach. It’s a really good thing, too, because in my line of work, sometimes I end up doing surveillance from my car for hours on end, drinking lukewarm deli coffee, and if I got motion sickness or an upset stomach easily, I’d be in real trouble. My sister gets terribly nauseous just riding in the passenger seat of a car, and she takes those little motion sickness pills all the time, but me? Never. The last time I took anything for my stomach was probably... gosh, years and years ago, when I had food poisoning from this terrible seafood place downtown that isn't even open anymore. They got shut down for health code violations, which didn't surprise me one bit. 

So, yeah, no, nothing like that recently. Not a single new pill. Why do you ask? Can those types of medicines make a person completely unable to sit still? Because I'm definitely not taking anything that would cause this.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly mentions being 'completely unable to sit still,' indicating significant physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a very long, rambling response with multiple unnecessary details to a simple yes/no question about medication, demonstrating excessive talking.

turns.doctor_question: When you get up from your seat, is it because you feel driven to do it to relieve a specific intrusive thought or fear?
turns.patient_response:
An intrusive thought or fear? Oh, gosh, no, no, it’s nothing like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, if I don't stand up right this second, something terrible is going to happen," or like I have to go check if the stove is on or the door is locked. I mean, my sister has a friend who does that, she has to check the locks exactly three times before she can even pull out of her driveway, and if she loses count, she has to start all over again. It sounds absolutely exhausting, honestly, but no, what I'm dealing with isn't like that. 

It’s really just this... this overwhelming physical urge. It's like my legs just decide they've had enough of the chair, completely independent of whatever my brain is doing. I'll be sitting there, listening to a client talk about a cheating spouse or a missing asset, and my mind is completely focused on the conversation, I'm taking notes, I'm fully engaged in the work—but my body just sort of rebels. It's almost like a pressure builds up in my muscles, and standing up is the only way to release the valve. 

There's no fear involved, no bad thoughts I'm trying to push away. I just suddenly feel like if I don't move, I'm going to jump out of my own skin. It's purely physical, just this restless energy that completely takes over. So, yeah, no intrusive thoughts or anything like that. Just an absolute inability to keep my bottom glued to the seat, no matter how much I want to or how inappropriate the timing is.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes an absolute inability to stay seated, even when they want to or when it is inappropriate.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient reports an overwhelming physical urge, restless energy, and feeling like they will jump out of their skin if they don't move.
symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly denies experiencing intrusive thoughts or bad thoughts they are trying to push away.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies that their need to move is driven by a need to prevent something terrible or perform checking rituals.

turns.doctor_question: Were you this unable to stay seated when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. Yes, I was exactly like this as a kid. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my mother about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes in her attic—she's finally downsizing, moving into a smaller condo, which is a whole other ordeal, let me tell you, trying to convince her to part with things she hasn't looked at since 1985. But anyway, we found this stack of my old report cards from elementary school.

And it was just... it was almost comical, reading them now. Every single one of them, from first grade all the way through middle school, basically said the exact same thing. The teachers would always write, "She’s very bright, grasps the material quickly," but then there was always the "but." "But she cannot stay in her seat," or "She has trouble waiting her turn." It was a constant theme. I mean, my mother still jokes about it. She says I treated every single classroom like a crime scene that I just had to pace through and investigate instead of just sitting at my desk like a normal student. 

I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade—she was this very strict, older teacher who always wore these brightly colored cardigans—she actually put a piece of masking tape around my desk. A literal square on the floor! And she told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape during lessons. It didn't work, of course. I'd just stand up and pace inside the little square, or I'd lean so far over the desk to talk to the kid next to me that I'd practically fall over. I just had this... this motor running inside me, even back then. I couldn't just sit and listen to the lesson. I had to be up, moving, checking out the pencil sharpener, looking out the window, seeing what the kid three rows over was drawing. So, yeah, this isn't a new thing at all. It's just that now, as a 49-year-old professional, it's a lot less cute and a lot more disruptive to my actual life and career.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted during class by extraneous stimuli like the pencil sharpener, the window, or other students.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms she could not stay in her seat during class, often standing up even when confined to a taped square.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes pacing through the classroom and being unable to sit still, indicating inappropriate restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes herself as having a 'motor running inside' her, matching the feeling of being driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient recalls that her childhood report cards consistently noted she had trouble waiting her turn.
